        SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY’S RESPONSE TO STAFF’S
              EXCEPTIONS TO CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION

           In accordance with the Commission’s November 5, 2026 Order Granting Leave to File

Responses to Exceptions, Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) responds to the

Commission Utility Division Staff’s (“Staff”) November 2, 2026 Exceptions (“Exceptions”) to the

Hearing Examiners’ October 23, 2026 Certification of Stipulation (“Certification”). For the

following reasons, the Commission should reject Staff’s Exceptions, particularly Staff’s novel and

unsupported proposal to condition approval of the Stipulation on multiple future compliance

filings.

  I.       INTRODUCTION

           Staff’s Exceptions largely repeat arguments that, after a four-day evidentiary hearing and

extensive post-hearing briefing, the Hearing Examiners considered and rejected. Those arguments

include objections to SPS’s future-test-year (“FTY”) forecasts and the burden of proof, 1 linkage

data, 2 forecasted jurisdictional allocators, 3 and bill impacts. 4 On these issues, the Hearing

Examiners held that (1) SPS complied with the FTY Rule requirements for updating data, 5 (2)

New Mexico law permits the use of forecasted jurisdictional allocators, 6 and (3) the record

supported the stipulated $90 million base-rate increase subject to specified changes. 7

           Staff now proposes, for the first time, another round of filings that would undermine the

finality of Commission ratemaking and turn the Signatories’ June 22, 2026 Comprehensive

Stipulation (“Stipulation”) on its head. Specifically, Staff asks the Commission to condition



           1
             Staff’s Exceptions Nos. 1–2.
           2
             Staff’s Exceptions Nos. 3–5.
           3
             Staff’s Exceptions Nos. 6–7.
           4
             Staff’s Exception No. 8.
           5
             Certification ¶¶ 133–134.
           6
             Id. ¶¶ 72–93.
           7
             Id. ¶¶ 141–142.

                                                   1
 approval of the Stipulation on SPS filing, before its new rates take effect, (1) its completed 2026

V-1 financial load forecast, (2) its current resource-adequacy position, and (3) actual linkage data

for July 1 through November 20, 2025. Staff would also require SPS to calculate how each of these

future submissions would affect its FTY revenue requirement and cost allocations among

jurisdictions and customer classes, and present the results as adjustments under 17.1.3.19(C)

NMAC. 8 Staff then proposes additional review and comments by Staff and intervenors, subjecting

rates to refund pending that review, and potentially postponing the Commission’s decision.

       The Commission should reject this proposal for at least three reasons. First, Staff’s proposal

would turn the routine filing of approved rates into a second, unending rate case in violation of the

Public Utility Act and the Commission’s FTY Rule. Rather than implement the Commission’s

decision, the proposed filings would invite renewed challenges to the revenue requirement and

cost allocations already litigated without a clear framework for review. Staff identifies no authority

for reopening those issues through this filing process. The Commission should decide Staff’s

objections on the record before it, not create a second rate case following the conclusion of this

one.

       Second, Staff’s alternative proposal would force the Commission to resolve another round

of disputed evidence as the November 30, 2026 suspension deadline approaches. Staff offers no

workable schedule for reviewing the additional filings, resolving any resulting disputes, and

establishing final rates before that deadline. Its proposal would leave rates in limbo, subject to

refund for an undefined period.

       Third, Staff’s compliance-filing proposal would deprive the Signatories of the finality the

Stipulation meant to secure, undermining New Mexico’s policy in favor of settlement. The


       8
           Staff’s Exceptions at 24–25.


                                                  2
 Signatories negotiated a $90 million increase as part of an agreement whose terms are expressly

interdependent and non-severable. 9 Staff would leave that bargain open to ongoing challenges even

after the Commission approves it, even though any order inconsistent with the Stipulation would

allow any Signatory to withdraw from the agreement.

            Accordingly, the Commission should reject Staff’s Exceptions and proposed alternative

relief, resolve the remaining Exceptions on the existing record, and approve the Stipulation as

filed.

 II.        ARGUMENT

       A.        Staff’s alternative proposal conflicts with the FTY Rule’s requirements, would
                 delay final rates without a defined process in violation of the PUA, undermines
                 the Stipulation, and is contrary to the public interest.

                         1. Staff’s alternative proposal conflicts with the FTY Rule’s established
                            updating requirements.

            As already thoroughly briefed and argued, the FTY Rule expressly permits utilities to rely

on forecasts to set rates in a FTY case and establishes procedures for updating filings as

information changes. 10 SPS followed those procedures, including by submitting its Comprehensive

List of Revisions on March 20, 2026. The Hearing Examiners considered SPS’s subsequent

changes and found no violation of the Rule’s updating requirements. 11

            Staff’s alternative proposal would subvert this framework by imposing additional updating

requirements after the evidentiary hearing. Rather than apply the Rule’s established procedures for

material revisions, comprehensive lists of revisions, and subsequent corrections, Staff would

require SPS to submit new, rolling forecasts and calculations for further review and potential rate

adjustments. Nothing in the FTY Rule authorizes this additional process. Indeed, Staff goes so far


            9
              Stipulation ¶ 2.7(b).
            10
               See 17.1.3.18–.19 NMAC.
            11
               Certification ¶¶ 126–134.

                                                    3
 as to propose amending the Rule to require ongoing updates and reconciliations. 12 The

Commission can certainly open a rulemaking docket if it would like to do so, but Staff should not

be permitted to remedy its perceived deficiencies in the Rule by selectively imposing new FTY

requirements on one utility.

       Staff’s approach would also produce absurd results for utilities in FTY cases. Forecasts

inherently change as new information becomes available. If every change required another round

of filings, objections, and Commission review, FTY rate cases would continue indefinitely. The

Commission should apply the updating requirements already in place, which SPS followed, rather

than impose the open-ended compliance process Staff proposes. The Commission should reject

Staff’s proposed alternative relief.

                       2. Staff’s alternative proposal would delay final rates without a defined
                          process in violation of the PUA.

       New Mexico law favors final, predictable utility rates and establishes specific requirements

that apply to the processing of rate cases. With respect to applications to implement new rates, the

PUA expressly provides: “If the commission determines a hearing is necessary, it shall suspend

the operation of the proposed rates before they become effective but not for a longer initial period

than nine months beyond the time when the rates would otherwise go into effect, unless the

commission finds that a longer time will be required, in which case the commission may extend

the period for an additional three months.” 13 Section 62-8-7(C) of the Public Utility Act directs the

Commission to hear and decide rate cases “with reasonable promptness,” while the New Mexico

Supreme Court has long embraced policies that promote the predictability and stability of utility




       12
            Staff’s Exceptions at 24–25.
       13
            NMSA 1978, § 62-8-7(C).

                                                  4
 rates. 14 Finality in the administrative context depends on whether the Commission “has in fact

finally resolved the issues,” not merely whether it has issued an order labeled final. 15

       Staff’s proposed alternative relief would undermine these requirements. It would condition

approval of the Stipulation on additional evidence, further challenges to SPS’s revenue

requirement and cost allocations, and another round of Commission review. Staff also proposes

making rates subject to refund and postponing the Commission’s final decision. 16 In effect, the

Commission would approve the Stipulation while leaving its central financial terms unresolved.

       Staff also offers no workable timetable for its compliance-filing framework. The

suspension period for SPS’s new rates expires November 30, 2026. Staff does not explain how the

Commission could receive and evaluate the additional filings, consider objections, and resolve any

resulting disputes before that deadline. Nor does Staff explain how long SPS’s rates would remain

subject to refund. Although the Commission may authorize interim rates in certain circumstances,

doing so here would merely postpone the resolution of disputed issues the parties have already

litigated. The Commission should decide those issues now, rather than leave SPS and its customers

uncertain about the rates that will ultimately apply.

                   3. Staff’s alternative proposal would undermine the Signatories’
                      negotiated compromise and is contrary to the public interest.

       New Mexico law favors settlement of contested utility proceedings. The Commission has

consistently applied that policy by evaluating whether a stipulation (1) resulted from serious

bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties; (2) benefits customers and the public interest

when viewed as a whole; and (3) violates any important regulatory principle or practice when




       14
          See El Paso Electric Co. v. N.M. Pub. Regul. Comm’n, 2026-NMSC-014, ¶¶ 13, 25–27.
       15
          N.M. Indus. Energy Consumers v. N.M. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 1991-NMSC-018, ¶ 24.
       16
          Staff’s Exceptions at 24–25.


                                                    5
 viewed as a whole. 17 Ultimately, the issue before the Commission is whether the Stipulation

produces fair, just, and reasonable rates. 18 In making that determination, the Commission must

evaluate the negotiated result, not whether each provision reflects the position any particular party

advocated during litigation.

        Staff’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief acknowledges that the Commission must evaluate a

comprehensive stipulation as an “integrated package,” 19 but Staff’s alternative proposal here would

do the opposite. The Signatories negotiated a $90 million base-rate increase as part of an agreement

resolving numerous disputed issues. Requiring SPS to recalculate the revenue requirement using

updated forecasts and other information, then inviting further challenges to those calculations,

would reopen the very disputes the Signatories resolved.

        Nor could the Commission simply preserve the remaining provisions while reconsidering

the stipulated increase. Section 2.7(b) makes the Stipulation’s terms “interdependent and not

severable” and permits any Signatory to withdraw if the Commission issues an inconsistent order.

If adopted, Staff’s proposal threatens the entire agreement by leaving the Stipulation’s central

financial term open to further litigation. This is not in the interest of SPS, its customers, or the

public. The Commission should evaluate the Stipulation as written, not require the parties to

negotiate another agreement later.




        17
           Case No. 20-00238-UT, Final Order Adopting Certification of Stipulation ¶¶ 6–7 (Feb. 16, 2022); Case
No. 24-00270-UT, Final Order ¶ 34 (Oct. 30, 2025); Certification ¶¶ 28–29.
        18
           Certification ¶¶ 25–29.
        19
           Staff Initial Br. at 5.

     B.        Staff’s remaining exceptions provide no basis to reject the Stipulation.

                1. Staff’s novel jurisdictional allocation theory does not establish that SPS
                   will “double-recover” across New Mexico and Texas (Exceptions Nos. 6–
                   7).

         As the Hearing Examiners recognized, New Mexico law expressly allows utilities to use

forecasted jurisdictional allocators in a FTY rate case. 20 Texas law differs from New Mexico law

in numerous respects, including with respect to the selection of test years. Nothing requires SPS

to use identical test years or allocation methods in New Mexico and Texas. 21 The relevant question

is not whether SPS can use projected data, but rather whether the resulting New Mexico rates are

fair, just, and reasonable.

         Staff uses its Exceptions as yet another opportunity to advance its unsupported theory that

different allocation methods somehow create unlawful double recovery. Indeed, Staff goes so far

as to characterize the Certification as “simply stating that it was legal for SPS to over-recover.” 22

This plainly mischaracterizes the Certification, which recognized that differences between state

ratemaking methods and periods may cause temporary over- or under-collection, but that

possibility does not establish that New Mexico rates are unreasonable. 23

         Staff’s arithmetic adds nothing to this cursory analysis. Staff simply adds New Mexico’s

forecasted share of system costs (49.56%) to Texas’s historical share (55.46%) and concludes that

the 105.02% total shows double recovery. What Staff fails to account for is that forecasted and

historical allocators come from different test periods. Adding them together does not establish

what SPS has recovered, or will recover, let alone that SPS will recover the same costs twice.

Staff’s proposed $47.7 million revenue deficiency also rests on an inconsistent calculation: it



         20
            NMSA 1978, § 62-6-14(D); 17.1.3.18 NMAC.
         21
            Certification ¶¶ 72–75.
         22
            Staff’s Exceptions at 7.
         23
            Certification ¶ 74.

                                                   7
 counts New Mexico’s projected load growth when calculating revenues but ignores that growth

when allocating costs.

       Staff then renews its discussion of the Commission’s Final Order in Case No. 25-00066-

UT, insisting that that decision – which addressed resource approvals under the CCN statute –

governs the allocation of shared system costs here. The Final Order in Case No. 25-00066-UT

covered a broad scope of issues. What it did not cover was the use of forecasted allocators in a

Future Test Year case. Staff identifies no new evidence or legal authority supporting its

jurisdictional allocation theory, which the Hearing Examiners considered and rejected. The

Commission should do the same.

               2. Staff’s speculation about SPS’s revisions to data in its original application
                  does not establish that SPS violated the FTY Rule (Exceptions Nos. 3–5).

       Staff’s remaining Exceptions fail to establish any violation of the FTY Rule or an error that

materially affects the stipulated $90 million increase. As explained above, 17.1.3.19 NMAC

establishes procedures for revising a FTY application as information changes. SPS followed those

procedures, and the Hearing Examiners found no violation of the Rule. 24

       Staff again challenges SPS’s use of forecasted linkage data for periods preceding its

Application and its failure to incorporate subsequent changes in resource-adequacy information.

The Hearing Examiners considered both objections. 25 Staff identifies no adjustment to SPS’s

revenue requirement resulting from the allegedly outdated linkage data. Nor does a change in

SPS’s capacity-deficiency estimate establish an error in its financial load forecast. The two

measure different things, as SPS explained in its post-hearing briefing. 26 And, Staff failed to

present any testimony challenging SPS’s load forecast.


       24
          Id. ¶¶ 136–140.
       25
          Certification ¶¶ 99–134.
       26
          SPS Post-Hearing Response Brief at 10–12.

                                                      8
         Staff also argues that SPS’s approximately $7.8 million in revisions, combined with

another $1 million in hypothetical adjustments, could exceed the FTY Rule’s $8.77 million

materiality threshold. The problem with this argument is that Staff identifies no $1 million in

additional adjustments. 27 Although SPS’s projected capacity deficiency changed, Staff never

establishes that changes to SPS’s projected capacity deficit would affect SPS’s revenue

requirement by that amount, or at all. The Hearing Examiners separately found that the record

supported the stipulated $90 million increase, subject to specified adjustments. 28 Staff offers no

basis to disturb that finding.

                   3. The Hearing Examiners did not shift the burden of proof to Staff
                      (Exceptions Nos. 1-2).

        Staff’s burden-of-proof argument 29 mistakes the Hearing Examiners rejecting its evidence

for shifting the burden of proof. The Hearing Examiners correctly recognized that SPS bears the

burden of proving that its proposed rates are just and reasonable and that the Signatories must

support the contested Stipulation. 30 They then considered the evidence, found that a preponderance

of the evidence supported the stipulated $90 million increase, and recommended that the

Commission approve the Stipulation.

        Staff objects because the Hearing Examiners also found that Staff failed to support its

preferred jurisdictional allocation methodology and other objections. Those explain why Staff’s

arguments failed. They do not shift the burden of proof. That is, SPS presented sufficient evidence




        27
             Staff’s Exceptions at 13–14.
        28
            Certification ¶¶ 141–142.
         29
            New Mexico courts have recognized that the term “burden of proof” encompasses two distinct
concepts: the burden of persuasion and the burden of production, or of coming forward with evidence. See
Gemini Las Colinas, LLC v. N.M. Tax’n & Revenue Dep’t, 2023-NMCA-039, ¶¶ 19, 26–28, 531 P.3d 622
(citing Strausberg v. Laurel Healthcare Providers, LLC, 2013-NMSC-032, ¶ 24, 304 P.3d 409). The latter
burden can shift throughout an administrative proceeding while the former cannot. Id.
         30
            NMSA 1978, § 62-8-7(A); Certification ¶¶ 25, 34–35.

                                                   9
 to support the stipulated increase. Staff failed to undermine that evidence. Staff clearly disagrees

with how the Hearing Examiners weighed the evidence. This does not establish that the

Certification applied the wrong legal standard.

                    4. Staff repeats its bill-impact arguments without showing that the
                       Hearing Examiners erred (Exception No. 8).

        Staff again argues that its proposed $47.7 million revenue deficiency would produce lower

customer bills than the stipulated $90 million increase. Of course it would. That reductive

comparison proves nothing about whether the stipulated rates are just and reasonable. The Hearing

Examiners rejected Staff’s revenue-deficiency calculation and considered the Stipulation’s rate

design, customer impacts, and affordability provisions. Staff identifies no error in those findings

that warrants rejecting the Stipulation.

III.    CONCLUSION

        For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should reject Staff’s Exceptions and approve

the Stipulation in its entirety.
